## Twelve fifths almost make seven octaves

Stack twelve pure fifths and you land almost exactly seven octaves up. Almost.
Multiply by `3/2` twelve times and you overshoot by about a quarter of a
semitone: nothing at all on one chord, and a disaster once you want to play in
all twelve keys. That gap is the *Pythagorean comma*, and every tuning system
ever built is a decision about where to hide it.

*Equal temperament* hides it by spreading it evenly. Divide the octave into
twelve identical multiplicative steps, each with the ratio `2 ** (1.0 / 12)`,
and twelve of them give you an exact `2:1` octave. What you give up is that
almost no other interval keeps its pure small-number ratio any more.

The program puts that compromise next to the alternative. One major triad uses
the ratios `1:1`, `5:4` and `3:2`. The other uses equal-tempered offsets of 0, 4
and 7 semitones. On paper they're the same chord. So what does a quarter of a
semitone, spread across twelve keys, actually sound like?

## Why this example can't use a sine

Lesson 5 used `synth :sine` and was right to. Here it would destroy the entire
demonstration, so it's worth being explicit about why.

The audible difference between just and equal-tempered intonation comes almost
entirely from *partials that nearly coincide*. Take the root at 220 Hz. Its
fifth harmonic sits at 1100 Hz. A pure `5:4` third is 275 Hz, and its fourth
harmonic is also 1100 Hz, exactly. An equal-tempered third is 277.18 Hz, whose
fourth harmonic is 1108.7 Hz. Those two land 8.7 Hz apart, and 8.7 Hz is a
shimmer you can hear.

A sine wave has one partial and nothing else. Take away the harmonics and you
take away the phenomenon, leaving two tones that are 13.7 cents apart in
separate passes, which nobody can reliably identify. So the example below uses
`:saw`, which carries every integer harmonic, at a reduced amplitude for
headroom.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 60

root_hz = 220.0
just_ratios = [1.0, 5.0 / 4, 3.0 / 2]
equal_offsets = [0, 4, 7]

define :play_frequencies do |frequencies|
  frequencies.each do |frequency|
    # :saw carries all integer harmonics. The partials are the point here.
    synth :saw, note: hz_to_midi(frequency), amp: 0.22,
      attack: 0.05, sustain: 4, release: 0.5
  end
  sleep 5
end

just = just_ratios.map { |ratio| root_hz * ratio }
equal = equal_offsets.map { |steps| root_hz * (2 ** (steps / 12.0)) }
puts "just:  #{just.map { |hz| hz.round(2) }}"
puts "equal: #{equal.map { |hz| hz.round(2) }}"
play_frequencies just
play_frequencies equal
```

The just triad sits still. Its partials coincide exactly, so there's nothing to
beat and the chord locks into place. The equal-tempered triad shimmers, and the
shimmer has two speeds in it: roughly 8.7 pulses per second from the third, and
a much slower undulation of about 0.7 per second from the fifth, whose second
harmonic misses the root's third harmonic by only three-quarters of a hertz.

If you hear nothing on the first pass, you're not doing it wrong. Sustain each
chord longer and listen to the region well above the notes you played.

## Change one thing

1. Change `synth :saw` back to `synth :sine` and run both chords again. This is
   the control, and it should be striking: the difference you just heard largely
   disappears. Where was the effect living, if not in the notes you played?

2. Restore `:saw`, then lengthen `sustain` to 8 and `sleep` to 9. Slow beating
   needs time to complete a cycle. At 0.7 Hz, the fifth's undulation takes about
   a second and a half to swing through once.

3. Restore the original timing and move the root from 220 to 330 Hz. The
   formulas don't change, but every beat rate scales with the frequencies, so
   the shimmer speeds up by half again.

## What each system buys

Tuning maps symbolic intervals onto physical frequency ratios, and each system
protects something different. Ratio-based intonation makes the local
relationships exact. Equal temperament makes transposition uniform: four
semitones always multiplies frequency by the same amount, from any starting
pitch you like.

The equal-tempered formula closes because `2 ** (1.0 / 12)` raised to the
twelfth power is exactly 2. A stack of pure `3:2` fifths preserves a different
invariant, and twelve of those don't equal seven exact doublings. Neither system
is a broken version of the other. They satisfy different constraints, and you
can't have both.

The major third is where the numbers diverge most. The pure third is exactly
`5/4` of the root; the equal-tempered one is the fourth power of the semitone
ratio, landing 13.7 cents sharp. Those two thirds never sound together in this
program, so they don't beat against each other. Each simply forms a slightly
different relation with its own root and fifth. If the full triad hides the
difference, play root and third alone, then restore all three tones. Isolation
finds the relation; the complete chord puts it back in context.

Sonic Pi's note numbers are equal-tempered keyboard addresses. Explicit hertz
values let you step outside that mapping, which is exactly what this program
does. Keeping both representations visible heads off a common confusion: `:e4`
names a keyboard location. It promises nothing about a pure `5:4` relationship
with any particular C.

Lesson 7 holds pitch and oscillator completely still and varies amplitude
through time, which turns the envelope itself into the musical object.

## Take it further

Print both triads to two decimal places and calculate the hertz difference
between their thirds. Then print `(1.5 ** 12) / (2 ** 7)` and convert it to
cents with `1200 * Math.log2(...)`. You should get about 23.5, which is the
comma from the opening paragraph, now a number on your screen.

Add one more calculation: for each pair of nearly-coinciding partials, print the
expected beat rate as the absolute difference in hertz. Then audition both
chords in Sonic Pi 5 through the same synth, amplitude and envelope, and try to
count the pulses. If your count is anywhere near the printed rate, you've
connected an arithmetic prediction to something your ears did independently.
That's the whole method of this book in one exercise.
